Kubernetes (usually written K8s) is an open-source system for running containerized applications across a group of machines, called a cluster. Instead of you logging into each server and starting containers by hand, you describe what you want running, and Kubernetes works to make that true and keep it true.

The basic idea is **declarative desired state**. You write a manifest, usually YAML, that says something like "I want three copies of this web container, each with 512 MB of memory, reachable on port 80." You send that to the API server, which is the front door to the cluster. The API server stores the desired state in etcd, a consistent key-value database that holds the cluster's whole configuration.

The cluster is split into two roles. The **control plane** makes decisions. Its main parts are the API server, etcd, the scheduler, and the controller manager. The **worker nodes** run the workloads. Each node has a kubelet, an agent that talks to the control plane and makes sure the containers it is assigned are running, plus a container runtime such as containerd, and kube-proxy, which handles network rules so traffic reaches the right containers.

The smallest unit Kubernetes manages is a **Pod**, which wraps one or more closely related containers that share an IP address and storage. You rarely create Pods directly. More often you create a **Deployment**, which says how many Pod replicas you want and how to update them. A Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet creates the Pods.

The heart of how it works is the **reconciliation loop**. Controllers constantly compare the actual state of the cluster with the desired state stored in etcd. If you asked for three replicas and only two are running, the controller creates another Pod. The scheduler watches for Pods that have no node yet and picks a suitable node based on available CPU, memory, rules, and affinity settings. The kubelet on that node then pulls the image and starts the container, and reports back. If a node dies, the controllers notice the missing Pods and recreate them on healthy nodes. This is why Kubernetes is described as self-healing.

For networking, Pods get their own IP addresses, but those change whenever a Pod is replaced, so a **Service** provides a stable name and IP in front of a changing set of Pods, and spreads traffic across them. Scaling, rolling updates, and rollbacks all work the same way: you change the desired state, and the controllers move the cluster toward it step by step.
